syllabus.clause: work T₁, span T∞, parallelism T₁/T∞

at.step: Work is the total number of additions — what one worker alone would take. Span is the longest chain of additions that must happen in order. Parallelism is work divided by span: the most speed-up any worker count can ever buy.
The identical additions, redrawn as one chain instead of a tree, have a span equal to their own work. Nothing about the operations changed — only the order they are allowed to run in.

A greedy schedule — one that never leaves a worker idle while a ready task waits — finishes within the work divided by the workers, plus the span. That guarantee holds for every greedy schedule, and lands within a factor of two of the best any schedule could possibly do.

The same sum DAG, greedily scheduled on one, a few, and many workers: the real step count always sits between the two laws’ floor and this bound — and once the worker count passes the span, more workers buy nothing further at all.

Each worker owns a deque: it pushes and pops its own end, running depth-first exactly as a lone worker would. An idle worker becomes a thief, picking another worker at random and taking from the far end of that worker’s deque — the oldest task there, the one most likely to still carry work beneath it.

For a fully strict computation — every dependency returning straight to its parent, the shape a plain recursive fork-and-join program already has — the expected running time on many workers is the work divided by the workers, plus a constant times the span: Brent’s bound again, reached with no coordinator at all.

syllabus.clause: as in Cilk, Rayon and Tokio

at.step: Cilk is the language this scheduler was designed for. Rayon’s join runs this exact protocol in Rust, warning that blocking one half on the other inside it can deadlock. Tokio also steals from per-worker queues, but for tasks that wait on the network, not a fork-and-join chain of pure computation — a different point on the same design.

at.quote: each worker has a local run queue plus a LIFO slot for message-passing locality; a global injection queue sits behind them, and idle workers steal half of a busy worker's queue.
